opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key insight is that we don't have to trust the AI system itself in order to get trustworthy guarantees about what it does. The approach I've been working on, which we sometimes call "guaranteed safe AI" or "safeguarded AI," separates the problem into a few components. You have a world model, which is a mathematical description of the relevant part of the world — say, an electrical grid, or a biochemical process, or a supply chain. You have a safety specification, which is a formal statement of what outcomes are acceptable or unacceptable. And then you have a verifier that checks whether a proposed action or policy, when run through the world model, actually satisfies the specification.

The reason world models can be a trustworthy basis is that they're auditable in a way that neural networks fundamentally aren't. A world model can be written in a language that human domain experts can read, critique, and refine. It can incorporate known physics, known engineering constraints, and — importantly — explicit representations of uncertainty. We're not asking for a perfect model of reality. We're asking for a model that's conservative in the right ways: one that captures the range of plausible behaviors, including the ones we're uncertain about, so that if a policy is safe across that whole range, we have good reason to believe it's safe in reality.

Now, there's an obvious objection, which is: aren't world models just going to be wrong? And of course they'll be imperfect. But the question is whether they're more trustworthy than the alternative, which is essentially trusting the judgment of a black-box system we can only evaluate empirically, through red-teaming and benchmarks. With a world model, the errors are inspectable. You can point at a specific assumption and say, "that's wrong, here's why." You can iteratively improve it. And you can use bounds — Bayesian credal sets, imprecise probabilities — so that the model says "I don't know" rather than confidently asserting something false.

The other piece is that we can use powerful AI to help build these world models, while still not having to trust that AI. The AI proposes model components, and they get checked — against data, against expert review, against consistency with other parts of the model. It's a bit like how a mathematician might use an AI to find a proof, but then the proof is checked by a proof assistant like Lean. The trust bottoms out in something small and verifiable, not in the capabilities of the frontier system.

So I'd say the deep reason is this shift from trusting the agent to trusting the evidence. If we can get to a place where AI actions in safety-critical domains come with a certificate — a checkable argument that, according to an auditable model of the world, this action keeps us within acceptable bounds — that's a much stronger foundation than hoping the system's values or dispositions happen to be right.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the core idea is that right now, when we talk about AI safety, we're mostly relying on things like training the model to behave well and then testing it on a bunch of examples and hoping that generalizes. And the problem is that for a sufficiently capable system, that's just not good enough. You can't test your way to a guarantee. You can only test your way to "we haven't found a failure yet."

So what I'm interested in, and this is the program we've been building at ARIA under the Safeguarded AI banner, is shifting the burden of trust away from the AI system itself and onto something we actually can scrutinize. And that something is a world model: a mathematical, explicit description of the environment the AI is going to act in, the dynamics of that environment, and the uncertainty we have about it.

The reason that's a more trustworthy foundation is that a world model, if it's written in a formal language, is an object you can inspect. Humans can read it, domain experts can argue about whether it's right, and crucially, you can do formal reasoning over it. So instead of asking "do we trust this neural network?", you ask "given this model of the world, and given this specification of what unacceptable outcomes look like, can we produce a proof that the proposed action, or the proposed policy, keeps us within bounds?" And then the thing you have to trust is the proof checker, which is a tiny piece of software that's been around for decades and is about as well understood as anything in computer science.

Now, the obvious objection is: the world model is wrong. All models are wrong. And that's true. But I'd say two things about that. First, the world model doesn't need to be a perfect predictor. It needs to be conservative. It needs to capture the range of things that might happen, including the things we're unsure about, as probability distributions or as bounded nondeterminism. If you model your uncertainty honestly and your proof goes through under that uncertainty, then you've got a guarantee that holds across all the worlds consistent with what you know. That's a very different and much stronger thing than a point prediction being accurate.

Second, the world model is a much better place to concentrate human judgment than the AI's weights are. Nobody can look at a trillion parameters and say "yes, this is fine." But a group of engineers and scientists absolutely can look at a model of a power grid, or an air traffic system, or a chemical process, and say "yes, this captures the physics, and here are the places where we're uncertain, and here's how conservative we've been about those." That's a kind of review that's actually feasible, and it's the kind of thing we already do in safety-critical engineering. We're just proposing to make it the load-bearing component.

And the last piece is that this is a setup where you can let the AI be arbitrarily capable without that capability being the thing you're worried about. The AI can propose whatever clever action it wants. If it can't come with a certificate that checks out against the world model and the spec, it doesn't get deployed. So the frontier system becomes a very powerful search engine for safe actions, rather than an agent whose intentions we have to reverse-engineer. That decoupling, to me, is the whole game.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the key is to distinguish trusting a model’s judgment from using a model as an explicit set of assumptions against which you can check a claim. I don’t want to ask an AI, “Is this action safe?” and take its word for it. I want it to produce a proposed action, together with an argument that we can independently verify about what that action would do.

A world model gives us a way to express that argument. It describes how the environment might evolve, how our actions affect it, and where we’re uncertain. Then we can ask whether a safety property holds across the possibilities represented by that uncertainty, rather than just in the single future the model considers most likely.

Now, there’s a very important caveat: a proof about a model is not automatically a proof about reality. If the model leaves out a relevant failure mode, formal verification won’t magically recover it. So the trustworthiness has to come partly from validating the model, partly from being conservative about its limitations, and partly from restricting actions when we can’t establish that those assumptions apply.

What makes this promising is that it turns a vague assurance into something explicit and inspectable: here are the assumptions, here is the safety condition, and here is the reasoning connecting them. That doesn’t eliminate the problem of understanding the world, but it gives us a much more disciplined way to connect our understanding to the actions we allow an AI to take.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that a world model gives you something explicit to reason about. If an AI proposes an action, you can ask: across the possible situations represented by this model, what could happen, and does any of that violate our safety constraints? That’s a much more precise question than asking another AI whether the action seems safe.

But there’s an important qualification: a proof about a model is conditional on that model adequately describing the relevant parts of the world. You can have a perfectly valid proof and still get a bad outcome because you left something out. So the model itself isn’t automatically a trustworthy foundation. You need evidence for its assumptions, and you need to represent uncertainty rather than just take the model’s most likely prediction as reality.

The approach I’m interested in is to make those assumptions and uncertainties explicit, then verify that an action is safe across the range of possibilities you haven’t ruled out. If you can’t establish that, the system needs to gather more information or choose a more conservative action. The value is that you turn a vague claim of safety into a structured argument whose assumptions you can inspect and challenge.
